title: Orders API errors and payment backlog on a Kubernetes cluster
context: On Sep 20 a 40-node Kubernetes cluster running an order platform showed ingress 502 errors for orders-api, a growing payment-worker backlog, and several other anomalies. Every pod resolves names through a node-local DNS cache (node-local-dns, one per node) that forwards cache misses to cluster CoreDNS. The reviewer must classify how the observed conditions relate to one another and choose follow-up actions.

entities.description: Per-node DNS cache daemonset; forwards cache misses to CoreDNS.
Order API; calls pricing-service over HTTP and inventory-service through an endpoint-cache sidecar; autoscaled by an HPA.
Price computation service called by orders-api.
Queue consumer that captures payments at an external payment gateway.

evidence.text: Ingress 502 rate for orders-api is 6% since 09:04 (baseline below 0.1%). All 502s are ingress upstream timeouts at 3 s.

08:50: planned Redis cache failover to a new primary node, completed 08:52. 08:58-09:03: node-local-dns daemonset rolled to chart 2.4.0 on all 40 nodes as a routine chart bump; release notes say 'cache settings are now templated; defaults aligned with upstream'.
node-local-dns rendered config, before and after chart 2.4.0: the cluster.local zone changed from 'cache 30' to 'cache 5'. Forwarding targets and all other zones are unchanged.

CoreDNS query rate 4,100 per second at 08:55, 23,500 per second at 09:05, then flat between 22,000 and 24,000 per second until 10:30. Each of the 4 replicas has a 1-core CPU limit; usage sits at the limit and 58% of CPU scheduling periods are throttled from 09:04.
Lookup latency from pods: p50 2 ms -> 40 ms, p99 12 ms -> 1.9 s from 09:04. 3.8% of lookups time out at 5 s.

Since orders-api v5.2 its HTTP client for pricing-service has keep-alive disabled (workaround for a connection-reuse bug), so every pricing call opens a new connection and resolves the pricing-service name. For orders-api requests slower than 1 s, 70-90% of span time is in dns.lookup before the pricing call.
"We reuse connections to pricing, so DNS isn't in our hot path."
"Nodes are averaging 35% CPU across the cluster. DNS can't be CPU-starved."
Failover completed 08:52. From 08:53 onward orders-api Redis command p99 latency is 1.1 ms (same as prior week) and the Redis error count is zero.

orders-api log volume rose from 1.2 GB/h to 9.8 GB/h from 09:05; 91% of the added lines are 'pricing call failed, retrying' warnings. Node disk utilisation stayed below 20%. The log shipper is asynchronous with a bounded in-memory buffer that drops on overflow.

The orders-api HPA scales on in-flight requests per pod (target 40). It scaled orders-api from 10 to 30 pods between 09:12 and 09:15; node count stayed at 40. The 502 rate per pod is similar for the original and the new pods. CoreDNS query rate did not change during or after the scale-out.
orders-api pods reject work above 64 in-flight requests. At 09:25, with 30 pods, average in-flight requests per pod was 58.

orders-api reaches inventory-service through an endpoint-cache sidecar that resolves each upstream name at most once per 60 s and reuses connections. Sidecar logs show about one lookup per upstream per minute throughout the incident. orders-api -> inventory-service p99 latency stayed at 35 ms, while orders-api -> pricing-service p99 (including connection setup) rose from 60 ms to 2.8 s.

payment-worker resolves the payment gateway hostname through cluster DNS on each capture attempt and retries a timed-out attempt up to 3 times. DNS timeouts appear in 4% of attempts from 09:04. Queue backlog grew from 200 to 14,000 messages by 09:40; capture attempts that did not hit a DNS timeout completed in normal time.

Two customers report being charged twice for orders placed between 09:20 and 09:30. Whether payment-worker reuses an idempotency key across retries is not documented. Gateway capture logs for the two orders have been requested and not yet received.

A single CoreDNS deployment revision at 09:40 both applied image patch 1.11.3 and raised the CPU limit from 1 to 2 cores per replica. By 09:45 DNS timeouts fell from 3.8% to 0.4% and throttling to 9%. Neither change was applied separately.

hypotheses.text: The node-local-dns chart 2.4.0 rollout is the origin of the orders-api 502s and the payment-worker backlog.
The 08:50 Redis failover is the origin of the orders-api 502s.
The orders-api scale-out increased load on CoreDNS.
payment-worker retries during DNS timeouts produced the two reported double charges.

edges.to: DNS latency in orders-api -> inventory-service calls

actions.text: Roll node-local-dns back to the previous chart version.
Cap the orders-api HPA at 10 replicas until the incident is resolved.
Lower the orders-api log level from INFO to WARN.
Fail the Redis cache back to its original primary node.
Remove the endpoint-cache sidecar from orders-api so all upstream calls use the same resolution path.
Obtain the payment gateway capture logs, including idempotency keys, for the two reported double charges.
